chapter_note.about: Dynamic programming solves a big problem by solving its smaller pieces first and writing each answer in a table. Every DP question has the same three parts: what a cell means, how it is built from earlier cells, and which cells are filled first. GATE seldom asks you to invent a DP from scratch. It gives you a recurrence or a small instance and asks you to fill the table, read one cell, or state the time.

gate_patterns: Complete or check a recurrence: you see a table with a blank (LCS, subset sum) and choose the missing case or a valid fill order. Six questions.
Fill a small table by hand and read one number: the best bracketing of a matrix chain, a knapsack or rod-cutting value, or a longest subsequence. Nine questions.

chapter_note.simple: Dynamic programming is what you do when a big problem is made of smaller copies of itself. You solve the smallest copies first, write the answers on a sheet, and build bigger answers by looking back at the sheet. You never solve the same small problem twice, which is far faster than trying every possibility. Every DP needs three things: what each box on the sheet means, how to make a box from earlier boxes, and an order that fills earlier boxes first. Exam questions usually give you a small case and ask you to fill the sheet and read one number.

cards.title: Recurrence, base case, fill order
cards.simple: Say you want to give someone exactly 6 rupees using the fewest coins. Instead of guessing, you work out the answer for 1 rupee, then 2, then 3, and write each answer on a sheet. When you reach 6, you only look back at answers that are already on the sheet, so you never solve the same small case twice. That sheet is the table, and filling it from small to big is dynamic programming. In exam words: pick the state, write the recurrence from smaller states, set the base case, and fill so every cell you read is already done.
cards.idea: Imagine making change for 6 rupees with coins of 1, 3 and 4, using as few coins as possible. Instead of guessing, solve the small amounts first: 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. Each bigger answer is built from answers you already wrote down. That habit is **dynamic programming**: break a problem into smaller copies of itself, solve each copy once, and keep the answers in a table.
cards.definition:
Every DP has three parts.

1. **State:** one sentence saying what a table cell holds. Here, dp[a] is the fewest coins that make amount a.
2. **Recurrence:** a formula that builds a cell from smaller cells.
3. **Base case:** the cells that depend on nothing. You fill them first.

$$dp[a]=1+\min_{c\le a}\,dp[a-c]$$

Symbols: a is the amount, and c is one coin value with c at most a. The cell dp[a-c] is the best answer for what is left after using that coin. The 1 counts the coin you just used. The base case is dp[0] = 0, because zero coins make amount 0.

DP applies when the same smaller questions repeat (overlapping subproblems) and the best answer is built from best answers of the parts (optimal substructure).
cards.intuition_full: Think of a spreadsheet where each cell has a one-line formula pointing at cells above or to the left. You never solve the whole sheet at once. You start at the cells that need nothing, which is the base case, and let every formula use what is already filled. The state is the label that says what a number means, the recurrence is the formula, and the fill order is the promise that no formula points at a blank cell. Without the table you would recompute dp[2] every time a bigger amount needs it. With the table each cell is computed once. Greedy fails because it commits to one choice, the biggest coin, without checking the others. The table checks every coin at every amount.

example.setup: Coins of value 1, 3 and 4. Find the fewest coins that make amount 6.
steps: State: dp[a] = fewest coins that make amount a. Base case: dp[0] = 0.
Recurrence: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a-1], dp[a-3], dp[a-4]), using only coins that are at most a.
example.answer: The fewest coins is 2 (3 + 3). Greedy, which grabs the biggest coin first, gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, so greedy is wrong here.

examples.setup: Coins of value 1, 3 and 4. Find the fewest coins that make amount 6.
steps: State: dp[a] = fewest coins that make amount a. Base case: dp[0] = 0.

examples.answer: The fewest coins is 2 (3 + 3). Greedy, which grabs the biggest coin first, gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, so greedy is wrong here.

examples.setup: A table T has rows 0 to 3 and columns 0 to 3. Row 3 and column 0 are all 1. Every other cell is T[i][j] = T[i+1][j] + T[i][j-1]. Which fill order is valid, and what is T[0][3]?
steps: T[i][j] reads the cell below it (row i+1) and the cell to its left (column j-1).
Filling rows from top to bottom fails. When you reach row 1, row 2 below it is still empty.
Filling rows from bottom to top works, each row left to right. The cell below and the cell on the left are always ready.
examples.answer: T[0][3] = 20. Valid orders go from the bottom row to the top, or column by column from the left with each column filled bottom to top. Top-down row order is invalid. The trap avoided is assuming that top-left to bottom-right works for every table.

examples.setup: Coins of value 4 and 6. Find the fewest coins that make amount 9.
steps: Base case: dp[0] = 0. Start every other cell at infinity, which means 'not reachable yet'.
Amounts 1, 2, 3 and 5 have no way in. For example dp[5] = 1 + dp[1] = infinity, since 5 - 6 is negative and the 6 coin is skipped.
dp[9] = 1 + min(dp[5], dp[3]) = 1 + min(infinity, infinity) = infinity.
examples.answer: Amount 9 cannot be made, because both coins are even. The cell stays at infinity. Had you started the cells at 0, dp[9] would wrongly come out as 1.

cards.why: Without a table you either recompute the same small cases again and again, or you grab a greedy choice that turns out wrong. In GATE: you get a recurrence with a blank or a half-filled table, and you must name the missing case, read one cell, or say which fill order is valid.
how: Say in one sentence what a cell means.
Write the recurrence using only smaller cells.
Fill the base cells first, usually dp[0] or the first row and column.
Check the fill order: every cell you read must already be filled.
Read the answer from the cell your state definition points to.
cards.mistake: Leaving out a base case, so the first real cells read empty values and every later cell is wrong. A second slip is reading a cell that is not filled yet, for example on the same diagonal. Write the base cells first, then check that every arrow points to an earlier cell.
edge_cases: Amount 0 needs 0 coins. This is the base case that every other cell is built on.
A coin larger than the amount is skipped (check c at most a first).
If no combination works, the cell stays at infinity. Report 'impossible', never 0.
Two different recurrences can solve the same problem. Any one whose arrows point only to filled cells is valid.
connections: Greedy works only when a local choice is provably safe (see Greedy). DP checks every choice.
Floyd-Warshall and Bellman-Ford are DP in disguise (see Shortest paths).
Recursion plus a memo table is the same DP read top-down (see Recursion).

check.q: Same coins 1, 3 and 4. What is dp[7]?
check.a: dp[7] = 1 + min(dp[6], dp[4], dp[3]) = 1 + min(2, 1, 1) = 2, using the coins 3 and 4.

check.q: Why is dp[0] = 0 in the coin problem?
check.a: Zero coins make amount 0, and every other cell is built on this cell. Without it the first coin cells would read empty values.

check.q: Coins 2 and 5, amount 3. What is dp[3]?
check.a: The coin 2 gives 1 + dp[1], and dp[1] is infinity because no coin makes 1. The coin 5 is too big. So dp[3] is infinity: impossible.

cards.title: 1-D DP: a table of length n
cards.simple: You walk past a row of houses, each with a few gifts at the door. You may not take from two houses side by side. At each house you ask one question: is it better to skip this house, or to take it and skip the one just before? You write the best total so far after every house, and the next number on your list only needs the last two. In exam words: a 1-D DP fills one row of answers, where each cell is built from the one or two cells just before it.
cards.idea: Picture a row of houses with a gift in each, and you may not take from two neighbours. The best haul for the first i houses either skips house i, or takes it and skips house i-1. So each answer depends on the two answers before it. A **1-D DP** is one row of answers built this way.
cards.idea_full: Picture a row of houses with a gift in each. You may collect gifts, but never from two neighbouring houses. Look only at the first i houses. The best haul either skips house i, or takes house i and skips house i-1. So the answer for i houses depends on the answers for i-1 and i-2 houses. A **1-D DP** is one row of answers, where each cell uses the cells just before it.
cards.definition:
Fibonacci, staircase counting, longest increasing subsequence and non-adjacent sums all fill one row dp[0..n-1].

$$dp[i]=\max\big(dp[i-1],\;dp[i-2]+a[i]\big)$$

Symbols: a[i] is the gift in house i, and dp[i] is the best total using houses 0 to i. The term dp[i-1] is the case where we skip house i. The term dp[i-2] + a[i] is the case where we take it, so house i-1 is off limits.

Other 1-D problems keep the shape and change the recurrence. Staircase ways: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. Longest increasing subsequence: dp[i] is the longest one that **ends** at element i, so dp[i] = 1 + the largest dp[j] over earlier j with a[j] < a[i].
cards.intuition_full: The houses problem looks like it needs every subset, but you only need to ask about the last house. Either it is in your haul or it is not. If it is not, the best haul is the best for the houses before it, dp[i-1]. If it is, its neighbour is banned, so the rest comes from houses up to i-2, plus the gift: dp[i-2] + a[i]. Those two cases cover everything, so the larger one is right. Each cell reads only the two cells to its left, which is why one left-to-right pass is enough. Picture a staircase where each step's height is set by looking one or two steps back. Fibonacci and staircase counting have the same look-back shape with a sum instead of a max.

example.setup: Gifts in five houses: a = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]. No two chosen houses may be neighbours. Find the largest total.
steps: Lay out two rows. The top row is the gift in each house. The bottom row, dp[i], will hold the best total using houses 0 to i.
Base cells. dp[0] = 2, because one house gives 2. dp[1] = max(2, 7) = 7, because with two houses you may take only one.
example.answer: The largest total is 12, from the houses with gifts 2, 9 and 1. The finished row is dp = [2, 7, 11, 11, 12].

examples.setup: Gifts in five houses: a = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]. No two chosen houses may be neighbours. Find the largest total.

examples.setup: The distance of an array is the minimum number of elements you must replace (with any integers) to make it non-decreasing. Find the distance of [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6].
steps: The elements you keep must already be in order, so they form a non-decreasing subsequence. You replace everything else. So distance = n - (longest non-decreasing subsequence).
Let d[i] be the longest non-decreasing subsequence that ends at index i. Then d[i] = 1 + the largest d[j] over earlier j with a[j] at most a[i], or 1 if there is none.
d[0] = 1 (the 3). d[1] = 1 (nothing before is at most 1). d[2] = 1 + max(1, 1) = 2 (the 4 follows 3 or 1).
d[3] = 1 + d[1] = 2 (the second 1 follows the first 1). d[4] = 1 + max(1, 1, 2, 2) = 3 (the 5).
The row is d = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4]. The longest subsequence has length 4, for example 3, 4, 5, 6.
examples.answer: The distance is 8 - 4 = 4. The trap avoided is reading only the last cell. Here the largest value happens to be 4 at both index 5 and index 7, so always take the maximum of the row.

examples.setup: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of [1, 5, 2, 3, 0].
steps: d[0] = 1 (the 1). d[1] = 1 + d[0] = 2 (the 5 follows the 1).
d[2] = 1 + d[0] = 2 (the 2 follows the 1; the 5 is bigger than 2, so it cannot come before).
d[4] = 1 (the 0 is smaller than everything before it).
The row is [1, 2, 2, 3, 1]. The last cell is 1, but the largest cell is 3.
examples.answer: The answer is 3 (the subsequence 1, 2, 3). Reading the last cell would give 1, which is wrong. For 'ending at i' tables, take the maximum of the whole row.

cards.why: A 1-D table replaces a search over every subset of houses with n quick steps. In GATE: you fill a short table for a longest increasing subsequence, a minimum number of replacements, or a count of ways, and read one number.
how: Say what dp[i] means: the best for the first i items, or the best sequence ending at item i.
Write dp[i] from earlier cells only.
Set the starting cells, usually dp[0], and dp[1] if the recurrence looks two steps back.
Fill left to right.
Pick the answer: the last cell, or the largest cell if dp[i] means 'ending at i'.
cards.mistake: For 'ending at i' tables such as the longest increasing subsequence, people read the last cell. The best subsequence may end earlier, so the answer is the largest value in the whole row.
edge_cases: Strict versus non-decreasing: use a[j] < a[i] for strict and a[j] <= a[i] for non-decreasing. Equal values change the answer.
All elements equal: strict LIS is 1, non-decreasing LIS is n.
One house or one element: only the base cell exists, so there is no dp[1] to fill.
Non-adjacent sum: skipping a house is always allowed, so a gift that hurts is simply not taken.
connections: LIS of an array with distinct values is the LCS of the array and its sorted copy.
Fibonacci and staircase counting are the same table with + instead of max. Plain recursion on them is exponential (see Recursion).
LIS also has an O(n log n) method, but GATE tables use the O(n^2) one.

check.q: Gifts a = [5, 1, 1, 5]. What is the largest non-adjacent total?
check.a: dp[0] = 5, dp[1] = max(5, 1) = 5, dp[2] = max(5, 5 + 1) = 6, dp[3] = max(6, 5 + 5) = 10. The answer is 10, from the two 5s.

check.q: A staircase has 4 steps. You climb 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time. How many ways reach the top?
check.a: ways[0] = 1, ways[1] = 1, ways[2] = 2, ways[3] = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, ways[4] = ways[3] + ways[2] + ways[1] = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. The answer is 7.

check.q: What is the longest strictly increasing subsequence of [2, 2, 3]?
check.a: d = [1, 1, 2]. The two equal 2s cannot both be used in a strictly increasing run. The answer is 2.

cards.title: LCS and edit distance
cards.simple: Two friends each wrote their favourite songs in order. You want the longest list of songs that appears in both lists, in the same order, skipping songs when you need to. You draw a grid with one list along the top and the other down the side. Where the two songs match, you take the score diagonally up-left and add 1. Where they differ, you copy the better score from the cell above or to the left. The bottom-right number is the answer. In exam words: LCS is the diagonal plus 1 on a match and the max of up and left on a mismatch, in time proportional to m times n.
cards.idea: A subsequence keeps letters in order but may skip some, so ACT is a subsequence of AGCT. The **longest common subsequence** (LCS) is the longest one that appears in both strings. Compare the strings prefix by prefix. Each table cell stores the answer for the first i letters of one string and the first j of the other.
cards.idea_full: A subsequence keeps letters in their order but may skip some. For example, ACT is a subsequence of AGCT. The **longest common subsequence** (LCS) of two strings is the longest one that appears in both. To find it, compare the strings prefix by prefix. A table cell remembers the answer for the first i letters of one string and the first j letters of the other.
cards.definition:
$$L[i][j]=\begin{cases}L[i-1][j-1]+1 & x_i=y_j\\\max(L[i-1][j],L[i][j-1]) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Symbols: L[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i letters of X and the first j letters of Y. The letters x_i and y_j are the i-th letter of X and the j-th letter of Y.

When they match, both letters join the answer, so take the diagonal cell L[i-1][j-1] and add 1. When they differ, one of them goes unused, so keep the better of the cell above and the cell to the left. Row 0 and column 0 are all 0, because an empty prefix shares nothing.

The table has (m+1)(n+1) cells with constant work each, so time is $\Theta(mn)$. Edit distance uses the same grid with a min over insert, delete and replace, and with base cells D[i][0] = i and D[0][j] = j.
cards.intuition_full: Lay the two strings side by side and draw a line between equal letters, with no lines crossing. The LCS is the most lines you can draw. Look at the last letters of the two prefixes. If they are equal, you can always draw that line and then solve the smaller problem without those letters, which is the diagonal plus 1. If they differ, at least one of them has no line. So drop the last letter of X (the cell above) or the last letter of Y (the cell to the left), and keep the better result. Row 0 and column 0 are zero because an empty string has nothing to line up. Edit distance is the same picture with costs: a match is free along the diagonal, otherwise you pay 1 for a replace (diagonal), a delete (up) or an insert (left).

example.setup: X = AGCT (rows) and Y = GACT (columns). Row 0 and column 0 are filled with 0 first.
steps: Row 0 and column 0 are all 0, because an empty prefix shares nothing. Every other cell reads its up, left or diagonal neighbour.
Row A. (A,G) is a mismatch: max(up 0, left 0) = 0. (A,A) is a match: diagonal 0 + 1 = 1. The next two cells are mismatches and copy the left value 1. Row: 0, 1, 1, 1.
Row G. (G,G) is a match: diagonal 0 + 1 = 1. Then (G,A) = max(up 1, left 1) = 1, and the rest are 1. Row: 1, 1, 1, 1.
Row C. (C,G) = max(up 1, left 0) = 1. (C,A) = max(up 1, left 1) = 1. (C,C) is a match: diagonal (G,A) = 1, plus 1 gives 2.
(C,T) is a mismatch: up (G,T) = 1, left (C,C) = 2. Keep the larger, 2.
Row T. (T,G) = 1, (T,A) = 1, (T,C) = max(up 2, left 1) = 2. (T,T) is a match: diagonal (C,C) = 2, plus 1 gives 3.
example.answer: The LCS length is 3. Two strings achieve it, ACT and GCT, and both appear in AGCT and in GACT.

examples.setup: X = AGCT (rows) and Y = GACT (columns). Row 0 and column 0 are filled with 0 first.

Row A. (A,G) is a mismatch: max(up 0, left 0) = 0. (A,A) is a match: diagonal 0 + 1 = 1. The next two cells are mismatches and copy the left value 1. Row: 0, 1, 1, 1.
Row G. (G,G) is a match: diagonal 0 + 1 = 1. Then (G,A) = max(up 1, left 1) = 1, and the rest are 1. Row: 1, 1, 1, 1.
Row C. (C,G) = max(up 1, left 0) = 1. (C,A) = max(up 1, left 1) = 1. (C,C) is a match: diagonal (G,A) = 1, plus 1 gives 2.
(C,T) is a mismatch: up (G,T) = 1, left (C,C) = 2. Keep the larger, 2.

Left branch: (C,C) is a match, so C, then (B,A) leads up to (A,A), a match A. This builds the string A C A.

No common letter: the whole table stays 0.
A cell holds a length. Different traceback paths can spell the same string or different strings.

Compare the strings prefix by prefix. Each table cell stores the answer for the first i letters of one string and the first j of the other.
cards.what_full:
A subsequence keeps letters in their order but may skip some. For example, ACT is a subsequence of AGCT. The **longest common subsequence** (LCS) of two strings is the longest one that appears in both. To find it, compare the strings prefix by prefix. A table cell remembers the answer for the first i letters of one string and the first j letters of the other.

$$L[i][j]=\begin{cases}L[i-1][j-1]+1 & x_i=y_j\\\max(L[i-1][j],L[i][j-1]) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

Symbols: L[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i letters of X and the first j letters of Y. The letters x_i and y_j are the i-th letter of X and the j-th letter of Y.

When they match, both letters join the answer, so take the diagonal cell L[i-1][j-1] and add 1. When they differ, one of them goes unused, so keep the better of the cell above and the cell to the left. Row 0 and column 0 are all 0, because an empty prefix shares nothing.

The table has (m+1)(n+1) cells with constant work each, so time is $\Theta(mn)$. Edit distance uses the same grid with a min over insert, delete and replace, and with base cells D[i][0] = i and D[0][j] = j.

1. Row 0 and column 0 are all 0, because an empty prefix shares nothing. Every other cell reads its up, left or diagonal neighbour.
2. Row A. (A,G) is a mismatch: max(up 0, left 0) = 0. (A,A) is a match: diagonal 0 + 1 = 1. The next two cells are mismatches and copy the left value 1. Row: 0, 1, 1, 1.
3. Row G. (G,G) is a match: diagonal 0 + 1 = 1. Then (G,A) = max(up 1, left 1) = 1, and the rest are 1. Row: 1, 1, 1, 1.
4. Row C. (C,G) = max(up 1, left 0) = 1. (C,A) = max(up 1, left 1) = 1. (C,C) is a match: diagonal (G,A) = 1, plus 1 gives 2.
5. (C,T) is a mismatch: up (G,T) = 1, left (C,C) = 2. Keep the larger, 2.
6. Row T. (T,G) = 1, (T,A) = 1, (T,C) = max(up 2, left 1) = 2. (T,T) is a match: diagonal (C,C) = 2, plus 1 gives 3.

**Answer:** The LCS length is 3. Two strings achieve it, ACT and GCT, and both appear in AGCT and in GACT.

*Answer:* Row A: (A,B) = 0, (A,A) = diagonal 0 + 1 = 1. Row B: (B,B) = diagonal 0 + 1 = 1, (B,A) = max(up 1, left 1) = 1. The length is 1.

cards.title: Matrix-chain multiplication
cards.simple: Say you must multiply a chain of big grids of numbers. Any grouping gives the same final answer, but some groupings take far more work, a bit like folding laundry in the right order so the pile never gets huge. To find the cheapest grouping, you decide where the very last multiplication happens and try every spot. For each spot you add the cost of the left part, the cost of the right part and the cost of joining them. You work out short chains first and build up to the whole chain. In exam words: matrix-chain DP tries every split k in m[i][j] and keeps the minimum, in time proportional to n cubed.
cards.idea: Matrices can be multiplied in any bracketing and the result is the same. The cost is not the same. A p by q matrix times a q by r matrix takes p·q·r multiplications. DP finds the cheapest bracketing by trying every place the last split could go.
cards.idea_full: You can multiply matrices in any bracketing, and the final matrix is the same. The work is not the same. Multiplying a p by q matrix with a q by r matrix takes p·q·r scalar multiplications. For a long chain, a good bracketing can save a lot. DP finds the cheapest one by trying every place where the last multiplication could split the chain.
cards.definition:
$$m[i][j]=\min_{i\le k<j}\big(m[i][k]+m[k+1][j]+p_{i-1}\,p_k\,p_j\big)$$

Symbols: matrix A_i has size p_{i-1} by p_i. The cell m[i][j] is the cheapest cost to multiply A_i through A_j. The number k is the split point: multiply A_i to A_k and A_{k+1} to A_j separately, then multiply those two results. That last product costs p_{i-1} · p_k · p_j. A single matrix costs 0, so m[i][i] = 0.

There are about n² cells and up to n splits each, so time is $\Theta(n^3)$ and space is $\Theta(n^2)$.
cards.intuition_full: Multiplication of matrices is associative, so every bracketing gives the same product. The cost is not the same, because a middle result can be big or small. Multiplying a tall thin column by a wide thin row gives a huge square, which then costs a lot to carry forward. The recurrence asks only about the last multiplication. Whatever the best bracketing is, one final multiplication joins A_i to A_k with A_(k+1) to A_j. Both sides should be bracketed as cheaply as possible on their own, so you add their best costs plus the cost of the join. You do not know k, so you try every one and keep the smallest. That is why you fill chains of length 2 first, then 3, then 4. A chain only reads shorter chains.

example.setup: Three matrices: A1 is 10×30, A2 is 30×5, A3 is 5×60. The dimension list is p = [10, 30, 5, 60].
steps: Single matrices cost nothing: m[1][1] = m[2][2] = m[3][3] = 0.
The smaller is 4500, at k = 2.
example.answer: The cheapest cost is 4500 scalar multiplications, with the bracketing (A1A2)A3. The other bracketing costs 27000, six times more.

steps: A1A2 costs 100 x 1 x 100 = 10,000 and gives a 100x100 matrix. A2A3 costs 1 x 100 x 1 = 100 and gives a 1x1 matrix.

how: Write the dimension list p0, p1, ..., pn. Matrix Ai is p(i-1) by p(i).
Chains of length 1 cost 0.
Fill chains of length 2, then 3, and so on. For each chain, try every split k and keep the minimum.
m[1][n] is the answer, and the winning k at each cell gives the bracketing.
For three or four matrices, skip the table and compare the few bracketings directly.

cards.title: Knapsack, subset sum, coins, rod cutting
cards.simple: You are packing a school bag that can only carry a certain weight. Each thing is either brought or left at home. You make a chart where each row means 'the things I have thought about so far' and each column means 'how much weight the bag can hold'. For each box you compare two options: leave the new thing at home, or bring it and use the leftover space for the earlier things. You always look at the row above, so nothing gets packed twice. In exam words: 0/1 knapsack K[i][c] is the max of the cell above and (value plus the cell above at c minus weight), in time O(nW).
cards.idea: You have a bag with a weight limit and some items, each with a weight and a value. For each item you choose: leave it or take it. The table stores the best value for every smaller bag and every shorter item list. This is **0/1 knapsack**, where each item is used at most once.
cards.idea_full: You have a bag that holds weight 5 and a few items, each with a weight and a value. You want the most value without going over the limit. For each item you make one choice: leave it, or take it. The table remembers the best value for every smaller bag and every shorter list of items. This is **0/1 knapsack**, where each item can be used at most once.
cards.definition:
$$K[i][c]=\max\big(K[i-1][c],\;K[i-1][c-w_i]+v_i\big)$$

Symbols: K[i][c] is the best value using only the first i items with capacity c. The numbers w_i and v_i are the weight and value of item i.

Skip item i: the best stays K[i-1][c], the cell directly above. Take item i, allowed only when w_i is at most c: you gain v_i and have c - w_i capacity left for the first i-1 items, which is K[i-1][c-w_i]. Row 0 is all zeros.

If an item may be reused, read the same row, K[i][c-w_i]. That is the unbounded version. Subset sum, coin change and rod cutting are variants. Time is $O(nW)$.
cards.intuition_full: Packing a bag with a weight limit means choosing, for every item, leave it or take it. Trying all subsets is 2^n. Instead ask a smaller question: with only the first i items and a bag of size c, what is the best value? For item i there are two choices. Leave it, and the answer equals the one with i-1 items. Take it, and you spend w_i of the bag, so the rest is the best you can do with i-1 items in the smaller bag. Reading the row above is what stops you taking an item twice. Reading the same row would let the item be used again, which is the unbounded problem. Greedy by value per weight can fail because the best-looking item can leave space that nothing else fits.

example.setup: Capacity 5. Items as (weight, value): item 1 = (2, 3), item 2 = (3, 4), item 3 = (4, 5).
steps: Row 0 means no items, so every cell is 0.
Item 1 (weight 2, value 3) fits once the capacity is 2 or more. The row becomes 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3.
Item 2, capacity 5. Skip: the cell above is 3. Take: 4 + K[1][2] = 4 + 3 = 7. Keep 7. The whole row is 0, 0, 3, 4, 4, 7.
Item 3, capacity 4. Skip: the cell above is 4. Take: 5 + K[2][0] = 5 + 0 = 5. Take wins. The row is 0, 0, 3, 4, 5, 7, because at capacity 5 skip gives 7 and take gives 5 + K[2][1] = 5.
The last cell, K[3][5], is the answer.
example.answer: The best value is 7, from items 1 and 2 (weight 2 + 3 = 5, value 3 + 4 = 7).

examples.setup: Capacity 5. Items as (weight, value): item 1 = (2, 3), item 2 = (3, 4), item 3 = (4, 5).

The last cell, K[3][5], is the answer.
examples.answer: The best value is 7, from items 1 and 2 (weight 2 + 3 = 5, value 3 + 4 = 7).

examples.setup: Capacity 8. Items as (weight, value): item 1 = (5, 60), item 2 = (4, 40), item 3 = (4, 40). A greedy method takes items by best value per weight. Compare it with the DP.
steps: Greedy ratios are 12, 10 and 10. It takes item 1 (weight 5). Only 3 units are left, and no other item fits. Greedy value: 60.
DP row 1 (item 1, (5, 60)): the cells for c = 0 to 4 are 0, and for c = 5 to 8 they are 60. Row: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 60, 60, 60, 60.
Row 3 (item 3, (4, 40)) at c = 8: skip gives K[2][8] = 60. Take gives 40 + K[2][4] = 40 + 40 = 80. Keep 80.
The last cell K[3][8] = 80, from items 2 and 3 (weight 4 + 4 = 8).
examples.answer: The best value is 80. Greedy by ratio gets only 60, so the gap is 20.

examples.setup: A single item has weight 3 and value 5. The capacity is 6. Find the best value for 0/1 knapsack, and then for the unbounded version.
steps: 0/1 reads the row above. Row 0 is all zeros, so row 1 is 0, 0, 0, 5, 5, 5, 5.
Unbounded reads the same row. K[1][3] = 5, so K[1][6] = max(K[0][6], 5 + K[1][3]) = max(0, 5 + 5) = 10.
examples.answer: 0/1 gives 5 because the item can be used once. Unbounded gives 10 because it can be used twice. Reading the wrong row turns one problem into the other.

cards.why: Greedy choices such as best value per kilo can fail, so you need the table. In GATE: you find the best value, count tied optimal sets by hand on a small instance, or state the table size and running time.

Fill row 0 with zeros.
For each cell, skip means copy the cell above. Take means v plus the cell one row up and w columns left, allowed only when w is at most the capacity.
Write the larger of the two.
The answer is the last row, last column. For ties, list the subsets by hand.
cards.mistake: Reading the same row for 'take'. That lets an item be counted twice, which is the unbounded problem. For 0/1, always read the row above.
edge_cases: An item heavier than the capacity cannot be taken, so copy the cell above.
Capacity 0: the value is 0, whatever the items are.
Subset sum is knapsack with value equal to weight. The question becomes whether some cell reaches the target exactly.
Ties: different sets can reach the same best value. The table gives the value, not how many sets reach it.
connections: Coin change and rod cutting are unbounded knapsack, which reads the same row (see Recurrence, base case, fill order).
Fractional knapsack is solved by greedy on value per weight. 0/1 is not (see Greedy).
O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial (see Cost of DP). Subset sum is NP-complete.

check.a: Items 1 and 3 weigh 2 + 4 = 6 and are worth 3 + 5 = 8. Items 1 and 2 weigh 5 and give only 7. All three weigh 9, which is too heavy. The answer is 8.

check.a: You can take the item twice, using weight 6, for value 10. A third copy would need weight 9. The answer is 10.

cards.title: DP on DAGs and grids
cards.simple: Imagine a city where every street is one-way and you may only go right or down. To count how many ways reach a corner, you add the number of ways to reach the corner above it and the number of ways to reach the corner to its left. A closed road adds zero. You start at the beginning, where there is exactly one way, and work outward so every number you need is already written down. The same trick works on any map of one-way roads with no loops. In exam words: on a grid or a DAG, a cell's value is the sum or best of its incoming cells, filled in topological order.
cards.idea: A robot walks from the top-left of a grid to the bottom-right, moving only right or down. Every path into a cell comes from the cell above or the cell to the left. So its number of ways is the sum of those two cells' ways. A **DAG** (a directed graph with no cycles) works the same way, if you handle each vertex after all its predecessors.
cards.idea_full: A robot walks from the top-left of a grid to the bottom-right, moving only right or down. Any path into a cell comes from the cell above or the cell on the left. So the number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach those two neighbours. A **DAG** (a directed graph with no cycles) works the same way. Handle the vertices in an order where every predecessor comes first.
cards.definition:
$$\text{ways}(r,c)=\text{ways}(r-1,c)+\text{ways}(r,c-1)$$

Symbols: r and c are the row and column, counted from 0. The start cell has 1 way. A blocked cell has 0 ways. Cells off the grid count as 0.

On a DAG, the rule for a vertex v combines the values of all vertices u with an edge u to v. Use a sum to count paths. Use a max or min to find the best path, adding or multiplying the edge weight. Process the vertices in topological order, which is an order where every edge goes forward.
cards.intuition_full: Think of counting routes in a city of one-way streets that only go right or down. You can reach an intersection only from the one above it or the one on its left. So the number of routes to it is the sum of the counts at those two. You never list the routes, you just carry counts forward. A blocked crossing contributes zero. The same idea works on any DAG, because the routes to a vertex come in through its incoming edges. The only rule is that every source of those edges is finished first, which is exactly a topological order. For best-route questions the sum becomes a max or min, and you add the edge cost on the way.

example.setup: A 3 by 3 grid, rows and columns numbered 0 to 2. The centre cell (1, 1) is blocked. Count the right-or-down paths from (0, 0) to (2, 2).
steps: The start cell is 1. Every other cell in the top row and left column has one way in, so each is 1.
The blocked centre cell (1, 1) has 0 ways.
example.answer: There are 2 paths. They go around the blocked centre, one along the top and right edges, one along the left and bottom edges.

examples.setup: A DAG has edges s-a (3), s-b (2), a-c (2), b-c (5), a-d (4), c-d (1), c-t (3), d-t (2). The quality of a vertex is the maximum over paths from s of the product of the edge weights. The source has quality 1. Find the quality of t.
steps: Choose a topological order: s, a, b, c, d, t. The vertex c needs a and b, d needs a and c, and t needs c and d.
examples.answer: The quality of t is 30. The traps avoided are starting the source at 0, which would make every product 0, and handling d before c.

steps: First row, running total: 1, 1 + 7 = 8, 8 + 8 = 16. First column: 1, 1 + 5 = 6, 6 + 2 = 8.
Greedy goes 1, 5, 2, 9, 6, which totals 23.
examples.answer: The minimum is 19, along 1, 5, 3, 4, 6. The greedy walk gets 23. Taking the smaller next cell is not the same as taking the cheaper whole path.

how: Order the vertices so every edge points forward (topological order).
Set the source cell: 1 for counting paths, 0 for cost, 1 for a product.
For each vertex, combine the values of its incoming edges: sum, min or max.
Blocked or unreachable cells stay 0 for counting, or infinity for a minimum.
Read the answer at the target vertex.
cards.mistake: Leaving the source cell unset, so every other cell stays at its default and the table is wrong. For a maximum product, the source quality is 1, not 0.
edge_cases: A blocked start or target cell gives 0 ways.
A single row or a single column has exactly 1 path.
An unreachable cell in a min-cost DP is infinity, not 0.
A graph with a cycle has no topological order, so this DP does not apply.
connections: Shortest paths in a DAG take one pass. Bellman-Ford is DP over the number of edges, and Floyd-Warshall is DP over the allowed middle vertices (see Shortest paths).
Topological order comes from DFS (see Graph traversal).
With no blocked cells, the number of right-or-down paths is a binomial coefficient, C(r + c, r).

cards.title: Cost of DP
cards.simple: Before you fill a DP table, count the boxes. Each box is one small problem, and filling a box takes a little work, so the total time is boxes times work per box. A table of 100 by 200 with one quick comparison per box takes about 20,000 steps. There is one catch with knapsack: the bag size W is a number, and a 10-digit number takes only 10 digits to write but would give a table with billions of columns. In exam words: time is states times work per state, and O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial because W is exponential in the number of bits that write it.
cards.idea: Before coding a DP, count the table. Each cell is one state. Time is the number of states times the work per state. A 6 by 5 table with one quick comparison per cell is about 30 steps.
cards.idea_full: Before you code a DP, count the table. Each cell is one state. The time is the number of states times the work to fill one state. A table with 6 rows and 5 columns and one quick comparison per cell is about 30 steps. So you count the cells, then multiply.
cards.definition:
$$\text{time}=(\text{number of states})\times(\text{work per state})$$

LCS has (m+1)(n+1) states at constant work each, so $\Theta(mn)$. Matrix chain has about n² states and up to n splits each, so $\Theta(n^3)$ time and $\Theta(n^2)$ space. Knapsack has (n+1)(W+1) states at constant work, so $O(nW)$.

In knapsack, W is a number someone types in, not the amount of input. Writing W takes only log2(W) bits. So the work grows exponentially with the length of the input. This is called **pseudo-polynomial** time.
cards.intuition_full: Before you code a DP, count its table. Every cell is a subproblem solved once, so the time is the number of cells times the work to fill one. LCS has m times n cells with one comparison each, and matrix chain has about n squared over 2 cells with up to n splits each, so n cubed. The space is the table size, unless a row only reads the row before it. Knapsack has a trap. The table is n by W, but W is a value, and a number W is written in only log2(W) bits. Making W one bit longer doubles W and doubles the table. So the time is polynomial in the number W but exponential in the length of the input. That is what pseudo-polynomial means.

example.setup: 0/1 knapsack with n = 10 items and capacity W = 1000.
steps: Count the states: (n + 1)(W + 1) = 11 × 1001 = 11,011 cells.
Work per state: compare two numbers, which is constant.
Total work is about 11,011 steps, which is $O(nW)$.
Now measure W as input. 1000 is below 2^10 = 1024, so it takes 10 bits.
Add 10 more bits: W = 1,024,000 takes 20 bits. The table has 11 × 1,024,001 = 11,264,011 cells, about 1000 times more.
example.answer: W = 1000 costs about 11,011 steps. Ten more input bits multiply the work by about 1000, so O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial.

steps: Each row reads only the row above it, so the length needs two rows of 3001 cells: 2 x 3001 = 6002 cells.
The time is still about 2000 x 3000 = 6,000,000 steps. Only the space shrank.
Reading back one actual subsequence needs the whole table.
examples.answer: The full table has 6,005,001 cells. The length alone needs only 6002 cells of space, while the time stays Theta(mn).

cards.why: Sizing the table is the first step of every DP question, and the follow-up 'what is the time?' becomes easy once you have it. In GATE: time and space for LCS, matrix chain and knapsack, and statements asking whether a bound is polynomial.
how: Write the table dimensions.
Estimate the work for one cell: constant, or a loop over k.
Multiply the number of states by the work per state.
Space is the whole table, unless only the previous row is ever read.
If a numeric value W sets the table size, call it pseudo-polynomial.
cards.mistake: Calling O(nW) polynomial. Polynomial time is measured against the length of the input, and W takes only log W bits to write. Adding one bit to W doubles its value, and the work.
edge_cases: Count the border row and column when a question asks for the exact number of cells. Ignore them inside Theta.
One loop of k per cell turns n^2 cells into n^3 work.
If W is a small fixed constant, O(nW) is just O(n).
Memoised top-down code fills only the states it reaches, but its worst case is the same.
connections: Subset sum is NP-complete, yet DP solves it in O(nW) when W is small (see Complexity).
Brute force over subsets is 2^n. The table replaces it with n times W.
Time for a recurrence like T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) without a table is exponential (see Recursion).

scenes.title: LCS table filled cell by cell

steps.caption: Row and column for the empty prefix are all 0. Every other cell will use its up, left or diagonal neighbour.
Row A: cell (A, A) is a match. Take the diagonal 0 and add 1. The other cells copy the larger neighbour.
Row G: (G, G) is a match, so diagonal 0 plus 1 gives 1.
Row C: (C, C) is a match. The diagonal holds 1, so this cell is 2.
Cell (C, T) is a mismatch. Compare up (1) and left (2) and keep the larger, 2. Arrows point to the subproblems it read.
Row T: (T, T) is a match. Diagonal 2 plus 1 gives 3. The bottom-right cell is the LCS length.

scenes.title: Non-adjacent sum filled cell by cell

objects.text: dp[i] = best total using houses 0 to i

steps.caption: Top row: the gift a[i] in each house i. Bottom row: dp[i], the best total using houses 0 to i. We fill it left to right.
Base cells. With one house the best is 2. With two houses we may take only one of them, so we take the 7.
House 2. Skip it and keep dp[1] = 7, or take it and add dp[0] = 2 to the gift 9, giving 11. Keep 11.
House 3. Skip it and keep 11, or take it: dp[1] + 3 = 10. Skipping wins, so dp[3] stays 11.
House 4. Skip it and keep 11, or take it: dp[2] + 1 = 12. Taking wins. The answer is 12, from the gifts 2, 9 and 1.

scenes.title: 0/1 knapsack table with arrows to subproblems

steps.caption: Row 0 is all zeros: with no items the value is 0. Each later row asks, for each capacity, whether to take the new item.
Item 1 (weight 2, value 3) fits once c is 2 or more, so the row becomes 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3.
Cell (item 2, c=5). Skip: copy the cell above, 3. Take: value 4 plus the cell above and 3 columns left, 3, giving 7. Keep 7.
Cell (item 3, c=4). Skip: 4. Take: value 5 plus the cell above at column 0, which is 0, giving 5. Take wins, so 5.
The last cell is the answer: best value 7, from items 1 and 2. The table has n rows by W columns, so O(nW) time.

scenes.title: Counting grid paths with a blocked cell

objects.text: moves: right or down.  X = blocked

steps.caption: A robot starts at the top-left and moves only right or down. X marks a blocked cell. Each cell will hold the number of ways to reach it.
The start cell has 1 way. Every other cell in the top row and left column has only one way in, from its single neighbour, so each is 1.
Cell (1, 2). Above it is 1 way. To its left is the blocked cell, 0 ways. So 1 + 0 = 1.
Cell (2, 1). Above it is the blocked cell, 0 ways. To its left is 1 way. So 0 + 1 = 1.
Cell (2, 2). Above is 1 and left is 1, so there are 2 ways. That is the answer.
